items.title: Ira Gitler interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995
items.q: and then you hear Louis Armstrong, he was really the

ctx.x: Tell us what he did for the trumpet and what he did for jazz.

Well I mean there had been soloists before, powerful soloists, of course we’ve all heard about Buddy Bolden and the cylinder, the Edison cylinder that’s never been found, but you know the people who played with him survived to talk about him and how powerful he was and great in his own way. But in listening to the records of the people who came up with him and started to record, and then you hear Louis Armstrong, he was really the

first great soloist in the music, using an incredible technique and power to bring forth the product of a mind that thought not only very musically but very humanly because I think he embodied all the feelings that people have. He stirred those feelings up, with just a phrase or a note or his rhythm. He did it all. And he really freed up I think the other musicians to think in a broader way, that they could do more. Not necessarily just the bravura thing, which he had, but that he was also telling a story,…
